subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: Border Lengths — Counting the Quilt's Edge

tasks_in_class.description: Tick the lace option (red 40 units / green 50 units / blue 25 units) that would cover the entire border of the quilt.
Find the perimeter of the following shapes. All sides of the following shapes are equal. (pentagon with 4 cm side; bowtie figure with 5 cm side)
Draw two rectangles each having the following perimeters. (a) 26 cm (b) 18 cm

time_bands.activity: Introduce the quilt-border story. Students examine the Opening context, p.142 ("tick the lace option … cover the entire border…") and discuss what 'going all the way around' means before writing an answer.

Students work on Let Us Do Q1, p.142 ("find the perimeter of the following shapes…."). They count equal sides, then multiply side-length by number of sides and record results, sharing strategies with a partner.

Students work on Let Us Do Q2, p.142 ("draw two rectangles each having the following perimeters…."). They plan on squared paper, draw rectangles and verify by summing all four sides, trying more than one pair of dimensions for each target.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who add only two sides instead of all four — prompt them to trace each side with a finger before adding. The idea that many different rectangles can share the same perimeter (established in the drawing task) will carry forward into the independence of area and perimeter explored later in the chapter. Encourage students to record at least two different rectangles for each target perimeter.

section_titles: Area via tiling — covering regions with shapes
periods.activity_title: Which Tile Fits? Covering Surfaces Without Gaps

tasks_in_class.description: Cover your table with triangles, circles, squares, and rectangles. Fill in blanks: which shapes cover without gaps, which leave gaps; count triangles / squares / rectangles covering each table; state the area in triangle / square / rectangle units.

Try to cover the top of your table without gaps and overlaps with the following objects of same size: (a) Notebooks (b) Lunch boxes (c) Pencil boxes (d) Maths textbooks. Which covered the region completely?

homework.description: Count how many square patches the grandmother used to make the rug shown in the picture.

time_bands.activity: Groups work on Tiling exploration, p.143 ("cover your table with triangles, circles, squares, and rectangles…."). Each group tiles with cut-out shapes, observes which leave gaps, counts tiles, and fills in the blanks together.

Groups work on Table cover with objects, p.143 ("try to cover the top of your table … with notebooks, lunch boxes, pencil boxes, maths textbooks…."). They predict, then test, and report which objects tile completely.

Whole-class discussion: students share findings, articulate why circles leave gaps and why flat rectangular objects tile fully, and arrive together at the idea that area is the region covered by tiles that fit without gaps.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often assume that any shape can tile a surface; the circle experiment produces the 'aha' that tiling requires no gaps. Keep the class discussion focused on the physical evidence rather than pre-announcing the rule — let the pattern emerge from the groups' reports. Rug patch count (p.143) is set as an individual home task so students revisit the counting idea with a pictorial example.
materials: Cut-out triangles, circles, squares, rectangles (pre-cut sets, one per group)
Students' notebooks, lunch boxes, pencil boxes, maths textbooks

section_titles: Comparing areas using grids and the unit square
periods.activity_title: How Many Squares? Tracing and Comparing on a Grid

tasks_in_class.description: Trace rectangles A, B, C on to a paper and cut them to find out which one has the largest area.
Look at the different tiles on Preetha's desk and answer how many of the following shapes will cover the desk. (a) Green triangles (b) Red triangles (c) Blue squares
Compare the areas of the two gardens given below on the square grid. Share your observations. Area of Garden A = ___ cm square; Area of Garden B = ___ cm square.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Trace and cut rectangles, p.144 ("trace rectangles A, B, C … and cut them to find out which one has the largest area…."). They overlap the cut-outs to rank them, then place each on a 1 cm grid to count squares.

Class examines Let Us Do (tiles), p.144 ("look at the different tiles on Preetha's desk…."). Students count green triangles, red triangles, and blue squares needed to cover the desk from the picture, noticing that the count varies by tile size.

Students complete Let Us Do Q1, p.145 ("compare the areas of the two gardens … on the square grid…."). They count unit squares in each garden, record the areas, and share observations — establishing the unit square as the standard measure of area.

periods.teacher_notes: Some students count only full squares and skip partial ones — prompt them to see that a square grid lets us count carefully and that we need a consistent unit. The garden comparison cements the idea that a square whose side is 1 unit gives exactly 1 unit square of area, which underpins all formula work later. Let the students articulate in their own words why the blue-square count differs from the triangle count before moving on.
materials: Plain paper for tracing and cutting
1 cm square grid sheets (two per student)

section_titles: Comparing areas using grids and the unit square
periods.activity_title: Palms and Leaves — Measuring Irregular Areas on a Grid

tasks_in_class.description: Trace your palm on the square grid and find the approximate area of your palm. Compare the area of your palm with your friend's palm. Who has a bigger palm?
Collect leaves of different kinds. Put them on a square grid and find their area. (a) Name the leaf with the largest area. (b) Name the leaf with the smallest area.

The following mats are made of square patches of equal size. How many square patches will be required to cover each mat? Would both mats require an equal or different number of patches? Trace and cut out a small square of the size given and find the area.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Let Us Do Q2, p.146 ("trace your palm on the square grid and find the approximate area…."). They press a flat hand, trace carefully, count full and partial squares using a consistent rule, and compare counts with a partner.

Students place collected leaves on grid paper for Let Us Do Q3, p.146 ("put them on a square grid and find their area…."). They count squares covered by each leaf and rank leaves from smallest to largest area.

Students read Let Us Do Q4, p.147 ("mats made of square patches … how many patches to cover each mat?"). They trace and cut the given square, use it to tile the printed mat outlines, count patches, and decide whether the two mats need the same or different numbers.

periods.teacher_notes: The key question for palm and leaf tracing is how to handle squares that are only partly covered — guide students to adopt the rule of counting a square if more than half is covered, keeping the method consistent across comparisons. Connecting palm-tracing (an irregular shape) to the unit-square idea from the garden comparison shows that the same grid method works for any outline, not just rectangles. Watch for students who confuse the perimeter of the leaf (the outline) with its area (the region inside).
materials: 1 cm square grid sheets (two per student)
Leaves of at least three different sizes (students collect before the unit)

section_titles: Area and perimeter relationship — same area, different perimeter
periods.activity_title: Same Area, Different Border — Discovering Independence

tasks_in_class.description: Tick the shapes with the same area. Find the perimeters of these shapes. What do you notice? Discuss.
Tick the shapes with the same perimeter. Find the areas of these shapes. What do you notice? Discuss.
Draw different shapes having the same area as the given shape. Write the perimeter of each shape. What do you notice? Discuss.

homework.description: Is the area of shape (a) less than the area of shape (b) given below? Discuss.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Let Us Explore Q1, p.147 ("tick the shapes with the same area … find the perimeters…."). They count grid squares to confirm equal areas, then sum side-lengths to find perimeters, recording both values in a table.

Students work on Let Us Explore Q2, p.148 ("tick the shapes with the same perimeter … find the areas…."). They reverse the process: confirm equal perimeters, then count grid squares for area, and discuss whether equal perimeter forces equal area.

Students draw on grid paper for Let Us Do Q1, p.149 ("draw different shapes having the same area as the given shape … write the perimeter of each…."). They create at least three different shapes of the same area, record each perimeter, and share the observation that perimeters differ.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common misconception here is that a larger perimeter implies a larger area. Pressing students to articulate 'same area, different perimeter — what does that tell us?' before giving the answer helps them own the insight. Let Us Do Q2 (p.150), comparing a square and a triangle on a grid, extends reasoning to non-rectangular shapes and is set as a home task so students have time to count carefully. Keep the class discussion focused on what stays the same and what changes each time.
materials: 1 cm square grid sheets (multiple per student)

section_titles: Area formula for rectangles and squares
periods.activity_title: Rows Times Columns — Deriving the Area Formula

tasks_in_class.description: Find the area of your classroom floor in square meters. Take the help of your teacher to measure the length and breadth of the floor. What is the perimeter of the classroom floor?
Find the area and perimeter of the following shapes (a)–(e) shown on a 1 cm square grid.

time_bands.activity: Teacher guides the class to look at a rectangle of unit squares and count them row by row, then column by column, arriving at the observation that rows × columns = total count — establishing Area = Length × Breadth from the concrete patch pattern before any formula is stated.

Students measure the classroom floor for Let Us Do Q1, p.151 ("find the area of your classroom floor in square meters … what is the perimeter?"). Groups measure length and breadth with a tape, compute area by multiplication, and compute perimeter by summing all four sides.

Students work on Let Us Do Q2, p.152 ("find the area and perimeter of the following shapes (a)–(e) … on a 1 cm square grid…."). For each shape they identify length and breadth, apply the formula, and also sum the boundary to confirm the perimeter.

periods.teacher_notes: Anchor the formula derivation in the quilt-and-patches image students already know — 6 rows of 4 patches each gives 24 without counting individually. Watch for students who confuse which dimension is length and which is breadth; the formula gives the same answer either way, so reassure them, but ensure they always label both. The classroom measurement step embeds the formula in a real, familiar space.

section_titles: Area formula for rectangles and squares
periods.activity_title: Measuring Real Objects and Solving Field Problems

tasks_in_class.description: Find the area and perimeter of the following objects. Use a scale or measuring tape to find the length and the breadth: (1) Cover of the Notebook (2) Newspaper (3) Blackboard (4) Ludo board (5–6 student choice).
Find the area of a rectangular field whose length is 42 m and breadth is 34 m.
The area of a rectangular garden is 64 square m and its length is 16 m. What is its breadth?

time_bands.activity: Students measure real objects for Let Us Do Q3, p.153 ("find the area and perimeter … cover of the notebook, newspaper, blackboard, ludo board…."). Pairs measure each object, apply the formula, and record area and perimeter in a table, choosing two additional objects of their own.

Students solve Let Us Do Q4, p.153 ("find the area of a rectangular field whose length is 42 m and breadth is 34 m…."). They write the formula, substitute values, and compute the product, writing the answer with the correct unit.

Students work on Let Us Do Q5, p.153 ("area of a rectangular garden is 64 square m and its length is 16 m … what is its breadth?"). They rearrange the formula — Breadth = Area ÷ Length — compute, and verify by multiplying back to check their answer.

periods.teacher_notes: The reverse problem (Q5) often exposes a procedural gap — students know Area = L × B but hesitate to divide. Encourage them to check by multiplying their found breadth by 16 to see if they recover 64. The real-object measurement task grounds the formula in tangible experience and builds confidence before the symbolic word problems. Common error: forgetting to write the unit as 'square metres' rather than 'metres'.

section_titles: Area formula for rectangles and squares
periods.activity_title: Breaking Apart an L-Shape — Composite Figure Area

tasks_in_class.description: Find the area of the following figure with the dimensions as marked in the figure. (L-shaped figure: total width 32 cm, top strip height 6 cm, lower portion height 12 cm)

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the L-shaped figure on the board with dimensions and asks students to suggest how to split it into two rectangles. Students sketch their partition lines on squared paper, discussing more than one way to split the figure.

Students work through Let Us Do Q6, p.153 ("find the area of the following figure … L-shaped figure: total width 32 cm, top strip 6 cm, lower portion 12 cm…."). They label each rectangle's length and breadth, apply the area formula to each part, add the two areas together, and write the total with correct units.

Pairs exchange books and verify each other's partition and computation. The class discusses whether a different partition gives the same total area, reinforcing that decomposition does not change the total region covered.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes subtract a missing rectangle from a larger rectangle rather than splitting — both strategies are valid; honour both and show that they give identical answers. The key check is whether the found dimensions of each sub-rectangle are consistent with the overall marked dimensions. Peer verification in the final phase catches arithmetic slips and builds the habit of checking computed answers.

periods.activity_title: Roll, Arrange, and Race to Perimeter 24

tasks_in_class.description: Take square tiles and a die. Roll the die, pick tiles equal to dots, arrange to make a shape, find the perimeter. Take turns adding tiles to the same figure till the perimeter becomes 24. The one who makes perimeter 24 wins.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates one round of Let Us Play, p.154 ("roll the die, pick tiles, arrange to make a shape, find the perimeter…."). A volunteer rolls, picks tiles, builds a shape on the desk, and the class counts the perimeter together by tracing each exposed edge.

Pairs play the full game from Let Us Play, p.154, taking turns rolling, adding tiles, and computing the running perimeter. Students record each shape's perimeter and discuss whether placing tiles so they share more sides helps or hurts the goal of reaching 24.

Whole-class discussion: students share the tile arrangements that gave the highest and lowest perimeters for the same number of tiles, articulating the relationship between how tiles are joined and the total perimeter — connecting back to the area-perimeter independence explored in the quilt border and garden activities.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes count corner points instead of edges — remind them to count each full exposed side of a tile, not its corner. The strategic question 'should I attach this tile along a long side or a short side?' surfaces the core idea that joining more sides reduces perimeter, and students who articulate this have grasped the deepest insight of the chapter. Encourage them to predict the perimeter before computing it, building estimation habits alongside the area and perimeter reasoning developed throughout the unit.
materials: Pencil and paper for recording perimeters

items.section_title: Area via tiling — covering regions with shapes
items.prompt: Riya wants to cover her rectangular tabletop completely without any gaps or overlaps using same-sized cut-outs. Which shape should she choose?

options.label: A
options.text: Circles

options.label: B
options.text: Ovals

options.label: C
options.text: Regular pentagons

options.label: D
options.text: Squares

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Squares, because they tile a flat surface with no gaps or overlaps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check which shape leaves no gaps when placed side by side on a flat surface.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not noticed that circles leave curved gaps between them and cannot tile a surface fully.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may think any regular polygon tiles; they have not tested that regular pentagons leave gaps.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused covering area with a shape that looks flat, without checking for gaps.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let them physically place cut-out shapes on a desk and observe; stretch: ask them to name one more shape that would also tile.

exercise.description: Cover your table with triangles, circles, squares, and rectangles. Fill in blanks: which shapes cover without gaps, which leave gaps; count triangles / squares / rectangles covering each table; state the area in triangle / square / rectangle units.

items.section_title: Comparing areas using grids and the unit square
items.prompt: Meena traces her hand on a 1 cm square grid. She counts 18 full squares and 6 squares that are more than half covered inside the outline of her hand. What is the approximate area of her hand? Write the area with its unit.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Approximately 24 square centimetres. (18 full squares + 6 more-than-half squares = 24 unit squares.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count full squares and add squares more than half covered to get the approximate area in unit squares.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student trace their own palm and physically count on the grid before writing; stretch: ask them to estimate whose palm is bigger if a friend's count is 21 and explain how they know.

exercise.description: Trace your palm on the square grid and find the approximate area of your palm. Compare the area of your palm with your friend's palm. Who has a bigger palm?

items.section_title: Comparing areas using grids and the unit square
items.prompt: Three rectangles P, Q, and R are placed on a 1 cm square grid. P covers 12 unit squares, Q covers 15 unit squares, and R covers 12 unit squares. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: All three rectangles have the same area.

options.label: B
options.text: P and R have the same area; Q has the largest area.

options.label: C
options.text: P has the largest area.

options.label: D
options.text: Q and R have the same area.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: P and R have the same area (12 unit squares each); Q has the largest area (15 unit squares).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the unit-square counts directly: equal counts mean equal areas; the larger count means the larger area.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused Q's count with R's, possibly mis-reading the grid or swapping labels.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not compared the counts carefully and assumed all three are equal.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has not read the counts correctly and ranked P highest despite P and R sharing the lowest count.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the three counts side by side and ask which two numbers are equal; stretch: ask the student to invent a fourth rectangle T that has an area between P and Q.

exercise.description: Trace rectangles A, B, C on to a paper and cut them to find out which one has the largest area.

items.prompt: A square quilt has a side of 8 units. Three lace rolls are available: yellow (28 units), orange (32 units), and pink (40 units). Which roll is just long enough to go exactly around the border of the quilt?

options.label: A
options.text: None of them fits exactly.

options.label: B
options.text: Orange (32 units)

options.label: C
options.text: Pink (40 units)

options.label: D
options.text: Yellow (28 units)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Orange (32 units). Perimeter of the square = 4 × 8 = 32 units.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the side length by 4 (number of sides of a square) and match the result to the lace lengths.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have added only three sides (3 × 8 = 24) or made an arithmetic slip.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have multiplied by 5 instead of 4, confusing a square with a pentagon.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student did not compute the perimeter correctly and concluded none matched.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw the square and label all four sides before adding; stretch: ask what side length a square would need to match the pink roll exactly.

exercise.description: Tick the lace option (red 40 units / green 50 units / blue 25 units) that would cover the entire border of the quilt.

items.prompt: Draw a rectangle on squared paper that has a perimeter of 20 cm. Label the length and breadth you chose. Now draw a different rectangle that also has a perimeter of 20 cm but different dimensions. Write the length and breadth of each rectangle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two pairs (length, breadth) where 2 × length + 2 × breadth = 20, for example (8 cm, 2 cm) and (6 cm, 4 cm), or (7 cm, 3 cm) and (5 cm, 5 cm). The dimensions must differ between the two rectangles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose a length, compute breadth as (20 ÷ 2) − length, verify that 2 × length + 2 × breadth = 20, then choose a different length for the second rectangle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student one dimension (e.g. length = 6 cm) and ask them to find the breadth; stretch: ask them to find the rectangle with the greatest possible area among all rectangles with perimeter 20 cm.

exercise.description: Draw two rectangles each having the following perimeters. (a) 26 cm (b) 18 cm

items.section_title: Comparing areas using grids and the unit square
items.prompt: Garden X covers 14 unit squares on a grid. Garden Y covers 9 unit squares on the same grid. Which garden has the larger area? By how many unit squares is it larger? Write your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Garden X has the larger area. It is larger by 14 − 9 = 5 unit squares.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the two unit-square counts and subtract the smaller from the larger to find the difference.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write both counts side by side and circle the bigger number; stretch: ask them to describe a Garden Z whose area is between X and Y.

exercise.description: Compare the areas of the two gardens given below on the square grid. Share your observations. Area of Garden A = ___ cm square; Area of Garden B = ___ cm square.

items.section_title: Area and perimeter relationship — same area, different perimeter
items.prompt: Shape P has an area of 12 unit squares and a perimeter of 14 units. Shape Q also has an area of 12 unit squares but a different arrangement. What can you say about Shape Q's perimeter?

options.label: A
options.text: Shape Q's perimeter can be different from 14 units.

options.label: B
options.text: Shape Q's perimeter must also be 14 units.

options.label: C
options.text: Shape Q's perimeter must be greater than 14 units.

options.label: D
options.text: Shape Q's perimeter must be less than 14 units.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Shape Q's perimeter can be different from 14 units. Equal area does not force equal perimeter.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Area and perimeter are independent; two shapes with the same area can have different perimeters depending on their arrangement.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student believes equal area forces equal perimeter — the core misconception this section addresses.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has over-generalised one example (perhaps a compact shape) to claim the perimeter must always be smaller.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has over-generalised from another example to claim the perimeter must always be larger.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw two different rectangles each covering 12 unit squares and measure both perimeters; stretch: ask them to find the arrangement of 12 unit squares that gives the smallest possible perimeter.

exercise.description: Tick the shapes with the same area. Find the perimeters of these shapes. What do you notice? Discuss.

items.section_title: Area and perimeter relationship — same area, different perimeter
items.prompt: On squared paper, draw three different shapes each with an area of 8 unit squares. Write the perimeter of each shape. What do you notice about the perimeters?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any three shapes covering exactly 8 unit squares, for example: a 1 × 8 strip (perimeter 18), a 2 × 4 rectangle (perimeter 12), and an L-shape of 8 squares (perimeter varies, e.g. 14). The perimeters are different even though the areas are the same.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw each shape on the grid, count unit squares to confirm area = 8, then count exposed edges to find the perimeter — observe that perimeters differ.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give one shape (a 2 × 4 rectangle) already drawn and ask the student to draw just one more with the same area; stretch: challenge them to find the shape with the largest possible perimeter for 8 unit squares.

exercise.description: Draw different shapes having the same area as the given shape. Write the perimeter of each shape. What do you notice? Discuss.

items.prompt: Arjun has 4 square tiles. He arranges them in a straight line (1 × 4 strip). His friend Priya rearranges the same 4 tiles into a 2 × 2 square. Whose arrangement has the larger perimeter?

options.label: A
options.text: Arjun's 1 × 4 strip has the larger perimeter.

options.label: B
options.text: Both arrangements have the same perimeter.

options.label: C
options.text: Priya's 2 × 2 square has the larger perimeter.

options.label: D
options.text: We cannot tell without measuring.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Arjun's 1 × 4 strip has the larger perimeter. Strip perimeter = 2 × (4 + 1) = 10 units; Square perimeter = 4 × 2 = 8 units.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count exposed edges for each arrangement: the strip has more exposed edges because tiles share fewer sides.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may think a compact square always has a larger perimeter, confusing compactness with boundary length.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student believes that rearranging tiles (keeping area the same) keeps the perimeter the same — the central misconception the game addresses.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student does not see that tile-edge counting gives a definite answer without a physical ruler.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw both arrangements on squared paper and trace the outside edges with a finger, counting each side; stretch: ask them to find a third arrangement of 4 tiles that gives a perimeter between 8 and 10.

exercise.description: Take square tiles and a die. Roll the die, pick tiles equal to dots, arrange to make a shape, find the perimeter. Take turns adding tiles to the same figure till the perimeter becomes 24. The one who makes perimeter 24 wins.

items.prompt: A regular hexagon has all sides equal. Each side is 7 cm long. What is the perimeter of the hexagon in centimetres?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the side length by the number of sides: 6 × 7 = 42 cm.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write out all six sides as 7 + 7 + 7 + 7 + 7 + 7 and add; stretch: ask the student to find what side length a regular hexagon would need for a perimeter of 54 cm.

exercise.description: Find the perimeter of the following shapes. All sides of the following shapes are equal. (pentagon with 4 cm side; bowtie figure with 5 cm side)

items.section_title: Area formula for rectangles and squares
items.prompt: A rectangular playground is 35 m long and 28 m wide. What is the area of the playground in square metres?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply Area = Length × Breadth: 35 × 28 = 980 sq m.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the rectangle on squared paper with labelled sides and count rows of 28; stretch: ask the student to also find the perimeter and state which measurement (area or perimeter) would help if they were fencing the playground.

exercise.description: Find the area of a rectangular field whose length is 42 m and breadth is 34 m.

items.section_title: Area formula for rectangles and squares
items.prompt: The area of a rectangular room is 48 square metres and its length is 8 metres. What is the breadth of the room in metres?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Rearrange Area = Length × Breadth to Breadth = Area ÷ Length: 48 ÷ 8 = 6 m.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write Area = Length × Breadth, substitute 48 = 8 × ?, and ask what number fills the blank; stretch: ask the student to verify by computing 8 × 6 and confirm it equals 48.

exercise.description: The area of a rectangular garden is 64 square m and its length is 16 m. What is its breadth?

items.section_title: Area formula for rectangles and squares
items.prompt: The figure below shows an L-shaped garden. Find its total area in square centimetres.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Part | Length (cm) | Breadth (cm) |
| Top rectangle | 20 | 5 |
| Bottom rectangle | 10 | 8 |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 180 square centimetres. Top rectangle: 20 × 5 = 100 sq cm. Bottom rectangle: 10 × 8 = 80 sq cm. Total = 100 + 80 = 180 sq cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split the L-shape into two rectangles, apply Area = Length × Breadth to each, then add the two areas.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student the two rectangles already drawn separately and ask them to find each area before adding; stretch: ask the student to find the perimeter of the full L-shaped figure using the given dimensions.

exercise.description: Find the area of the following figure with the dimensions as marked in the figure. (L-shaped figure: total width 32 cm, top strip height 6 cm, lower portion height 12 cm)
